passage:
[1] Every Tuesday at seven the Calder County council chamber fills with people who have come to speak for three minutes each about a culvert, a bus route, or a boundary on a zoning map. Behind the last row, at a folding table she brings in herself, Noor Haddad opens a machine the size of a bread box and waits for the gavel. Haddad — a realtime captioner who has worked in this chamber for nine years, writes onto a screen beside the dais every word that is spoken in the room, and she writes it inside a second.

[2] The machine is a stenotype, and it has no alphabet in the ordinary sense. Haddad presses several keys at once and the machine records the shape of an entire syllable, so a name that would cost eight strokes on a typewriter costs her one. The official record of a meeting is not the file Haddad keeps. What turns those shapes back into English is a dictionary of her own making, forty thousand entries long. The two backup files she keeps on a drive in her bag, along with the dictionary itself, travels to every meeting she works. The dictionary is hers, not the county's, and so are the files.

[3] Before each meeting Haddad loads the night's proper nouns into the dictionary, and the agenda gives her most of them: Ines Okonkwo, who lives on Barrow Road; Theodore Pham, of the Fifth Street Neighborhood Association; and a hydrologist from the state, whose office sends no agenda at all. The rest she takes from the room. One night in March the hydrologist, who, by the reckoning of the printed agenda, the chair had scheduled last, arrived first and spoke anyway. Haddad guessed the spelling of the hydrologist's surname from the sound of it and corrected the file at midnight.

[4] What Haddad writes on a Tuesday becomes a file the county posts online by Friday. The chamber has two clerks, and the official minutes are theirs, not Haddad's. Two people are hired for a Tuesday night: a sound technician and a captioner. The association that books the room covers the technician, and the county only pays Haddad by the hour. When the file and the minutes disagree, the clerk's version governs, and Haddad is not consulted about the difference. She has said she does not mind: the minutes are a summary, and a transcript is a different instrument. Meanwhile, the two records are not rival accounts of one night; they answer different questions.

[5] Two winters ago the chamber's microphones failed twenty minutes into a hearing on the culvert. One of the clerks moved to adjourn, and the chair was ready to agree. Haddad carried her table to the front of the room instead and kept writing, because a stenotype draws no power from the building and she could hear the speakers unaided. The council finishes the hearing that night, and the record it worked from afterward was hers.
prompt: In paragraph 1, which choice is most acceptable in place of "nine years,"?
explanation: A nonessential element dropped into the middle of a sentence must be enclosed by a MATCHING pair of marks, and this one was opened earlier in the same sentence by the dash after "Haddad", so it has to be closed with a dash: "nine years —". "nine years," closes with a comma an interrupter that a dash opened, leaving the pair mismatched and no signal that the interrupter has ended. A semicolon joins two independent clauses (or separates the internally punctuated items of a series), and what follows here is the sentence's own predicate, "writes onto a screen beside the dais", not a second clause. A colon must be preceded by a complete statement, and "Haddad — a realtime captioner who has worked in this chamber for nine years" supplies no predicate for "Haddad" and so is not one.
subskill: paired dashes closing a nonessential element

explanation: A relative pronoun takes its case from the job it does inside its OWN clause. That clause is "the chair had scheduled ___ last": the chair is the subject, "had scheduled" is the verb, and the relative pronoun is its direct object, so the objective form "whom" is required. "who" is the subjective form and would have to be the one doing the scheduling, which the chair is already doing. "whoever" and "whomever" are fused relatives that supply their own antecedent ("whoever built it" means "the person who built it"), so neither can follow the expressed antecedent "the hydrologist" that this clause modifies.

Nor does paragraph 2 need it early. Paragraph 2 is about how speech becomes text at all, not about what the resulting text counts for, and putting the standing of the file beside the mechanics of producing it interrupts the only thing the paragraph is doing.
subskill: relevance of a sentence to the paragraph's focus

passage:
[1] Every Tuesday at seven the Calder County council chamber fills with people who have come to speak for three minutes each about a culvert, a bus route, or a boundary on a zoning map. Behind the last row, at a folding table she brings in herself, Noor Haddad opens a machine the size of a bread box and waits for the gavel. Haddad — a realtime captioner who has worked in this chamber for nine years, writes onto a screen beside the dais every word that is spoken in the room, and she writes it inside a second.

[2] The machine is a stenotype, and it has no alphabet in the ordinary sense. Haddad presses several keys at once and the machine records the shape of an entire syllable, so a name that would cost eight strokes on a typewriter costs her one. The official record of a meeting is not the file Haddad keeps. What turns those shapes back into English is a dictionary of her own making, forty thousand entries long. The two backup files she keeps on a drive in her bag, along with the dictionary itself, travels to every meeting she works. The dictionary is hers, not the county's, and so are the files.

[3] Before each meeting Haddad loads the night's proper nouns into the dictionary, and the agenda gives her most of them: Ines Okonkwo, who lives on Barrow Road; Theodore Pham, of the Fifth Street Neighborhood Association; and a hydrologist from the state, whose office sends no agenda at all. The rest she takes from the room. One night in March the hydrologist, who, by the reckoning of the printed agenda, the chair had scheduled last, arrived first and spoke anyway. Haddad guessed the spelling of the hydrologist's surname from the sound of it and corrected the file at midnight.

[4] What Haddad writes on a Tuesday becomes a file the county posts online by Friday. The chamber has two clerks, and the official minutes are theirs, not Haddad's. Two people are hired for a Tuesday night: a sound technician and a captioner. The association that books the room covers the technician, and the county only pays Haddad by the hour. When the file and the minutes disagree, the clerk's version governs, and Haddad is not consulted about the difference. She has said she does not mind: the minutes are a summary, and a transcript is a different instrument. Meanwhile, the two records are not rival accounts of one night; they answer different questions.

[5] Two winters ago the chamber's microphones failed twenty minutes into a hearing on the culvert. One of the clerks moved to adjourn, and the chair was ready to agree. Haddad carried her table to the front of the room instead and kept writing, because a stenotype draws no power from the building and she could hear the speakers unaided. The council finishes the hearing that night, and the record it worked from afterward was hers.
prompt: In paragraph 4, which choice is most logical in place of "Meanwhile,"?
explanation: The sentence before this one states the ground: the minutes are a summary and a transcript is a different instrument. The sentence this transition opens states what follows from that ground — the two records are not rival accounts of one night but answers to different questions. The connective therefore has to mark a consequence, which is what "For that reason," does. "Meanwhile," marks two things going on at the same time and makes the second sentence a parallel event rather than something the first sentence establishes. "Even so," concedes the first sentence and turns against it, but the second sentence does not resist the first; it draws on it. "For instance," presents what follows as one case of a general claim just made, and the second sentence offers no instance of anything — it states a conclusion about the same two records the first sentence named.
